course.title: Computer Architecture
course.description: A ground-up tour of how a computer is built and how it runs a program, from single bits to multicore chips. The structure is adapted from the Computer architecture overview on Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia (CC BY-SA 4.0). All prose here is original, written to carry you from the von Neumann model through data representation, the processor, memory, pipelining, and parallel execution.

questions.prompt: The stored-program concept of the von Neumann model says that...
options: programs must be rewired by hand for each task
instructions and data share the same memory, encoded as numbers
a program can never change once it is written
data is always kept in a memory separate from instructions
questions.explanation: Both instructions and the data they act on live in one read-write memory, each stored as plain numbers - see 'What computer architecture is'.

questions.prompt: A byte is a group of how many bits?
questions.explanation: A byte is 8 bits, which can hold 2^8 = 256 distinct patterns.

questions.prompt: The hexadecimal digit F represents which decimal value?
questions.explanation: Hex uses 0-9 then A-F for 10-15, so F is 15.

questions.prompt: Which part of the processor actually performs arithmetic and logic?
questions.explanation: The arithmetic and logic unit does the computing; the control unit only directs it.

questions.prompt: The three phases of the basic instruction cycle are...
questions.explanation: The processor repeats fetch, then decode, then execute, for each instruction.

questions.prompt: Which statement about main memory (RAM) is true?
options: it keeps its contents without power
it is slower for the processor to reach than registers
it is the computer's permanent storage
questions.explanation: RAM is larger but slower to reach than the tiny, fast registers inside the processor.

questions.prompt: In two's complement, you negate a number by...
options: flipping every bit and then adding 1
questions.explanation: The two-step rule is: invert all the bits, then add 1.

questions.prompt: Which of these is the fastest for the processor to access?
questions.explanation: Registers sit inside the processor and are the fastest level of the memory hierarchy.

lessons.title: What computer architecture is and the von Neumann model
lessons.grammar_note: The processor is the arithmetic and logic unit plus the control unit; 'processor', 'central processing unit', and 'CPU' all name the same thing.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Explain what computer architecture studies and describe the von Neumann model that nearly every mainstream computer still follows. Warm-up: in your own words, what does it mean to say a program is stored the same way as the data it works on? Computer architecture is the study of how a computer is organized at the boundary between hardware and software: what parts exist, how they connect, and what rules the hardware promises to the programs that run on it. By the end of this lesson you will be able to name the five classic functional units, sketch how they exchange information, and say why keeping programs and data in the same memory was such a powerful idea. You will also be able to point out the one bottleneck this design creates, so that later lessons on caches and pipelines make sense as responses to a real problem rather than as isolated tricks.

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: The von Neumann model, named after a 1945 design report, describes a computer as five cooperating units: an input unit, an output unit, a memory, an arithmetic and logic unit, and a control unit. The last two together form the processor. The central claim, called the stored-program concept, is that both the instructions and the data they operate on live in the same read-write memory, encoded as plain numbers. Because an instruction is just a number, a program can read, write, and even generate other instructions, which is what makes a general-purpose computer so flexible. The control unit fetches one instruction at a time from memory, interprets it, and drives the other units to carry it out. Data and instructions travel back and forth along the same path between the processor and memory. This single shared path is both the elegance of the design and its weakness, since the processor often waits on memory. Almost every laptop, phone, and server you use is a refined von Neumann machine.

sections.heading: Key concepts & examples
sections.text: The stored-program idea replaced earlier machines that were rewired by hand for each task. Consider a tiny memory holding the numbers 1, 2, 3: the control unit might read location 0 and find the number 1, which by the machine's rules means 'load the next value', while another arrangement of the very same numbers could mean 'add'. Meaning comes from the rules, not from the bits themselves. The shared memory path creates the von Neumann bottleneck: because each instruction and each piece of data must cross the same connection, the processor frequently stalls while it waits for memory to respond. Much of modern design - caches, wider buses, pipelines - exists to soften this bottleneck. A common variant, the Harvard architecture, gives instructions and data separate memories and separate paths, which many small embedded chips and the inner cache levels of large processors adopt for speed. Example: a music player chip might keep its fixed program in one memory and the song samples in another, so fetching the next instruction never competes with streaming the audio data.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: 1) Name the five functional units of the von Neumann model. 2) Which two units together make up the processor? 3) What does the stored-program concept say about instructions and data? 4) In one phrase, what is the von Neumann bottleneck? 5) How does the Harvard architecture differ? 6) Why was replacing hand-rewiring with stored programs such an advance? Answers: 1) input, output, memory, arithmetic and logic unit, and control unit. 2) the arithmetic and logic unit and the control unit. 3) both are stored in the same memory, encoded as numbers, so the machine can treat an instruction as data and the reverse. 4) the single shared path between processor and memory forces instructions and data to take turns, so the processor often waits. 5) it uses separate memories and separate paths for instructions and for data, so the two no longer compete for one connection. 6) a single machine could run any program just by loading different numbers, instead of being physically rebuilt for each task.

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: believing the bits in memory are 'instructions' or 'data' by their nature - the same number means an instruction in one place and a value in another, purely because of the rules the processor applies. Mistake: assuming every computer separates program memory from data memory; the mainstream model deliberately shares them, and the separation is the exception. Mistake: imagining the control unit does the arithmetic; it only directs traffic, while the arithmetic and logic unit does the actual computing. Exit ticket: (a) In the von Neumann model, where do a program's instructions live relative to its data? (b) Which unit interprets each instruction and tells the other parts what to do? Answers: in the same shared memory, both encoded as numbers; the control unit, which fetches and decodes each instruction and then drives the arithmetic and logic unit, memory, and input and output units to execute it.

lessons.title: Data representation: binary, hex, two's complement, and logic gates
lessons.grammar_note: Write hexadecimal values with a leading 0x (as in 0xD6) so they are never mistaken for decimal numbers.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Read and write numbers in binary and hexadecimal, interpret negative numbers in two's complement, and trace the behavior of the basic logic gates. Warm-up: how many different values can a single group of eight bits hold? By the end you will be able to convert a small number between decimal, binary, and hex by hand, explain why hex is just a compact way of writing binary, work out the two's complement representation of a small negative number, and fill in the truth table for AND, OR, NOT, and XOR. These skills matter because everything inside a computer - instructions, text, images, sound - is ultimately a pattern of bits, and the arithmetic and logic unit you will meet later is built entirely out of gates. Getting comfortable with these notations now means the machine code and addresses in later lessons will read as ordinary numbers rather than intimidating strings of zeros and ones.

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: A bit is a single 0 or 1. A group of eight bits is a byte, and it can hold 2^8 = 256 distinct patterns. Binary is base 2: each position is worth twice the one to its right, so 1011 means 8 + 0 + 2 + 1 = 11. Hexadecimal is base 16, using the digits 0-9 and then A-F for the values 10-15. Hex is popular because each hex digit stands for exactly four bits, so long binary strings become short and readable: the byte 11010110 groups as 1101 0110, which is D6 in hex. To represent negative whole numbers, most computers use two's complement: to negate a number, flip every bit and add 1. In this scheme the leftmost bit signals the sign, addition and subtraction use the very same circuitry for positive and negative values, and there is exactly one pattern for zero. Logic gates are the physical building blocks: tiny circuits that take one or two bits in and produce one bit out according to a fixed rule.

sections.heading: Key concepts & examples
sections.text: Convert 13 to binary: 13 = 8 + 4 + 1 = 1101. Convert that to hex: 1101 is a single group worth 13, which is D, so 13 is 0x0D in a byte. Two's complement example in 8 bits: start with 5 = 0000 0101. Flip the bits to get 1111 1010, then add 1 to get 1111 1011, which represents -5. Check: 5 + (-5) should be 0000 0101 + 1111 1011 = 1 0000 0000, and the ninth bit falls off the end of a byte, leaving 0000 0000, which is zero. Logic gates: AND outputs 1 only when both inputs are 1; OR outputs 1 when at least one input is 1; NOT flips its single input; XOR outputs 1 when the two inputs differ. A tiny truth table for XOR: 0 XOR 0 = 0, 0 XOR 1 = 1, 1 XOR 0 = 1, 1 XOR 1 = 0. From these few gates, engineers build adders, comparators, and eventually the whole processor.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: 1) Write 25 in binary. 2) Convert the byte 1010 0011 to hex. 3) What decimal value is 0x1F? 4) Using 8-bit two's complement, represent -1. 5) Give the results of 1 AND 0, 1 OR 0, and NOT 1. 6) What is 1 XOR 1? 7) How many values can two bytes together represent? Answers: 1) 25 = 16 + 8 + 1 = 1 1001, or 0001 1001 in a byte. 2) 1010 is A and 0011 is 3, so 0xA3. 3) 0x1F = 1*16 + 15 = 31. 4) flip 0000 0001 to 1111 1110, add 1 to get 1111 1111, so -1 is all ones. 5) 1 AND 0 = 0, 1 OR 0 = 1, NOT 1 = 0. 6) 1 XOR 1 = 0. 7) 2^16 = 65536.

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: reading a two's complement byte with a leading 1 as a large positive number - if the machine treats it as signed, that leading 1 means the value is negative. Mistake: confusing a hex digit with a decimal one, for example reading 0x10 as ten when it is actually 16. Mistake: thinking XOR and OR are the same; they agree except when both inputs are 1, where OR gives 1 but XOR gives 0. Mistake: forgetting that the carry out of the top bit is simply discarded in fixed-width two's complement addition, which is exactly what makes the arithmetic wrap around cleanly. Exit ticket: (a) What is the two-step rule for negating a number in two's complement? (b) Why is hexadecimal convenient for writing binary? Answers: flip every bit, then add 1; because each hex digit maps to exactly four bits, so any binary string shortens by a factor of four with no loss of information.

lessons.title: The CPU and the fetch-decode-execute cycle
lessons.grammar_note: The program counter is a register, but a special one: it holds an address, not an ordinary data value.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Name the main parts of a central processing unit and walk through the fetch-decode-execute cycle that it repeats billions of times a second. Warm-up: before any arithmetic can happen, the processor must first get the instruction - where does it get it from? By the end you will be able to describe the roles of the arithmetic and logic unit, the registers, and the control unit; follow the program counter as it steps through memory; and explain what happens in each of the three phases of the basic instruction cycle. This is the heart of the course: once you can trace a single instruction from memory into the processor and back out as a result, the later topics - instruction sets, pipelines, and caches - are all refinements of this one loop. Keep the von Neumann model from the earlier lesson in mind, because the cycle is simply that model in motion.

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: The processor contains three key pieces. The arithmetic and logic unit performs calculations - addition, subtraction, comparisons, and bitwise logic. Registers are a small set of very fast storage slots inside the processor that hold the values being worked on right now; there are only a handful, but they are far quicker to reach than main memory. The control unit orchestrates everything, reading each instruction and sending signals that tell the other parts what to do. A special register called the program counter holds the memory address of the next instruction. The processor runs a simple loop forever. Fetch: copy the instruction at the address in the program counter from memory into the processor, then advance the program counter. Decode: the control unit works out what the instruction means and which registers or memory it touches. Execute: the arithmetic and logic unit or another unit actually carries it out, perhaps writing a result back to a register or to memory. Then the loop repeats with the next instruction.

sections.heading: Key concepts & examples
sections.text: Picture a program that adds two numbers. Suppose register R1 holds 7 and register R2 holds 5, and memory location 20 holds the instruction that adds R2 into R1. If the program counter currently reads 20, the fetch phase copies that instruction into the processor and bumps the program counter to 21. The decode phase recognizes the operation as addition and identifies R1 and R2 as the operands. The execute phase sends 7 and 5 into the arithmetic and logic unit, which returns 12, and the result is written back into R1. On the next turn of the loop, the program counter reads 21 and the whole process repeats for whatever instruction lives there. Two details matter. First, each phase may take one or more clock ticks; the clock is a steady pulse that keeps the parts in step. Second, some instructions change the program counter directly - a jump instruction loads a new address into it, which is how loops and decisions redirect the flow of a program.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: 1) Which register holds the address of the next instruction? 2) In which phase does the arithmetic and logic unit do its work? 3) What is a register, and why is it faster than main memory? 4) After fetching an instruction, what normally happens to the program counter? 5) How does a jump instruction change the ordinary flow? 6) Name the three phases of the instruction cycle. Answers: 1) the program counter. 2) the execute phase. 3) a small, very fast storage slot inside the processor; it is faster because it sits right next to the arithmetic and logic unit rather than out across the memory path. 4) it advances to point at the following instruction. 5) it writes a new address into the program counter, so the next fetch pulls from somewhere else, which is how loops and branches work. 6) fetch, decode, execute.

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: thinking the processor runs a whole program in one step - it actually grinds through one instruction at a time, repeating the same short loop. Mistake: confusing registers with main memory; registers are a tiny, fast scratchpad inside the processor, while main memory is large and slower and sits across the shared path. Mistake: assuming the program counter only ever counts upward; jumps and branches rewrite it, which is what makes decisions and loops possible. Mistake: believing the control unit performs the arithmetic, when in fact it only decodes and directs, leaving the calculation to the arithmetic and logic unit. Exit ticket: (a) List the three phases of the instruction cycle in order. (b) What does the program counter hold, and when does it change? Answers: fetch, decode, execute; it holds the address of the next instruction, and it changes after every fetch and again whenever a jump or branch loads a new address into it.

questions.prompt: Which two units together form the processor?
options: the arithmetic and logic unit and the control unit
the program counter and the data bus
questions.explanation: The arithmetic and logic unit plus the control unit make up the processor.

questions.prompt: The binary number 1011 equals which decimal value?
The byte 1101 0110 written in hexadecimal is...
questions.explanation: 1101 is D and 0110 is 6, so the byte is 0xD6.

questions.prompt: In the fetch phase of the instruction cycle, the processor...
options: writes a result back to memory
copies the next instruction from memory and advances the program counter
adds the contents of two registers
questions.explanation: Fetch brings the next instruction in and moves the program counter forward.

questions.prompt: Register R1 holds 7 and R2 holds 5; after an instruction that adds R2 into R1, R1 holds...
The 8-bit two's complement representation of -1 is...
questions.explanation: Flip 0000 0001 to 1111 1110, then add 1 to get 1111 1111.

lessons.title: Instruction set architecture, machine code, and assembly basics
lessons.grammar_note: Each assembly line usually maps to exactly one machine instruction, so counting lines roughly counts instructions.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Explain what an instruction set architecture is, see how machine code and assembly language relate, and read a few simple assembly instructions. Warm-up: if an instruction is just a number in memory, how does the processor know that one number means add and another means jump? By the end you will be able to define an instruction set architecture as the contract between hardware and software, describe the difference between the human-readable assembly form and the raw machine-code numbers the processor runs, and hand-trace a short assembly snippet that loads, adds, and stores values. You will also see why the same program can run on many chips that share one architecture, and why a program built for one architecture will not run on a different one without translation. This lesson connects the numeric world of the last two lessons to the programming world you already know.

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: An instruction set architecture, or ISA, is the set of instructions a processor understands plus the rules for using them: what operations exist, how many registers there are, how memory addresses work, and exactly how each instruction is encoded as a number. It is a contract. Any chip that implements the contract can run the same programs, which is why many different processors can all run software built for a common architecture. Machine code is the program expressed in that raw encoding - the actual numbers stored in memory. People almost never write those numbers by hand. Instead they write assembly language, a thin human-readable layer where each line usually corresponds to one machine instruction but uses names like ADD and LOAD and register labels like R1. A small program called an assembler translates assembly into machine code. Common architecture families differ in style: some keep a large, elaborate instruction set, while others deliberately keep instructions few and simple, trading richer single instructions for easier, faster hardware.

sections.heading: Key concepts & examples
sections.text:
Consider a short assembly snippet that computes 7 + 5 and stores the result:

LOAD R1, 7
LOAD R2, 5
ADD R1, R2
STORE R1, 100

Line by line: load the number 7 into register R1; load 5 into R2; add R2 into R1 so R1 now holds 12; store the contents of R1 into memory location 100. Each of these lines corresponds to a single machine instruction - a number whose bits encode both the operation and its operands. For instance, the ADD line might be encoded with a few bits meaning add, followed by bits naming R1 and R2. Change the bits that select the operation and the same slots now describe a subtraction. This is exactly the stored-program idea from earlier: the instruction is a number, and its meaning comes from how the architecture defines the encoding. Because the LOAD, ADD, and STORE names are far easier to read than the underlying numbers, programmers work in assembly and let the assembler produce the machine code.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: 1) In one sentence, what is an instruction set architecture? 2) What is the difference between machine code and assembly language? 3) What tool turns assembly into machine code? 4) Why can two physically different chips run the same program? 5) In the snippet above, what value sits in memory location 100 at the end? 6) Will a program built for one architecture run unchanged on a different one? Answers: 1) it is the contract defining the instructions a processor understands and how they are encoded. 2) machine code is the raw numeric encoding the processor executes, while assembly is a human-readable form where each line typically maps to one machine instruction. 3) an assembler. 4) because both implement the same instruction set architecture, so the same encoded instructions mean the same thing on each. 5) 12, the sum of 7 and 5 stored from R1. 6) no, not without translation or recompilation, since the encodings and instructions differ.

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: treating assembly language and machine code as the same thing - assembly is the readable text, machine code is the numbers the hardware actually runs, and the assembler bridges them. Mistake: assuming any program runs on any processor; it only runs on chips that share its instruction set architecture, unless it is recompiled or otherwise translated. Mistake: thinking a richer instruction set is always better; fewer, simpler instructions can let the hardware run faster and more predictably, which is a deliberate design trade. Mistake: forgetting that an assembly instruction and its machine encoding are two views of the very same instruction. Exit ticket: (a) What does an instruction set architecture define? (b) Which is human-readable, assembly or machine code, and what translates one into the other? Answers: the operations a processor supports, its registers, its addressing rules, and the numeric encoding of each instruction; assembly is human-readable, and an assembler translates it into machine code.

lessons.title: The memory hierarchy and locality
lessons.grammar_note: Say 'cache' for the small fast memory near the processor and 'storage' for the large persistent disk; they are not interchangeable.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Describe the memory hierarchy from registers down to storage and explain why caches work so well thanks to locality. Warm-up: why not simply build the whole computer out of the fastest possible memory? By the end you will be able to order the main levels of the hierarchy by speed and size, explain the cost and physics trade that forces the pyramid shape, define temporal and spatial locality, and describe what happens on a cache hit and a cache miss. This lesson explains the single most important reason real programs run fast or slow: whether the data they need is close to the processor when they need it. It builds directly on the von Neumann bottleneck you met earlier, because the entire hierarchy exists to hide the cost of reaching main memory. Understanding it will let you reason about performance long before you ever profile a program.

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: Memory forms a hierarchy, a pyramid that trades speed against size and cost. At the top sit the processor registers: a few dozen slots, extremely fast, but tiny in total. Below them are one or more levels of cache - small, fast memory on or very near the processor chip, typically labelled L1, L2, and L3 from smallest and fastest to larger and slower. Below the cache is main memory, the RAM, which is far larger but much slower to reach. At the bottom is storage - a solid-state or hard disk - which is enormous and persistent but slower again by a wide margin. You cannot build everything from registers because the fastest memory is expensive and physically must be small and close to the processor. The trick that makes the pyramid work is locality: programs tend to reuse the same data and to touch nearby data soon after, so keeping a small, recently used slice near the processor serves most requests quickly.

sections.heading: Key concepts & examples
sections.text: Locality comes in two flavors. Temporal locality means that if a program uses a value now, it is likely to use that same value again soon - think of a loop counter read on every pass. Spatial locality means that if a program uses one address, it will probably use nearby addresses soon - think of walking through an array element by element. Caches exploit both: when the processor needs a value, it first checks the cache. A cache hit means the value is there and is returned quickly. A cache miss means it is absent, so the processor must fetch it from the slower level below, and it brings along a whole neighboring block, betting on spatial locality. Example: summing a 1000-element array that fits in cache is fast because after the first miss brings in a block, the next several elements are already cached hits. By contrast, jumping randomly across a huge region defeats locality, causing miss after miss and forcing slow trips to main memory on nearly every access.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: 1) Order these from fastest to slowest: RAM, registers, disk storage, cache. 2) What does temporal locality mean? 3) What does spatial locality mean? 4) What is the difference between a cache hit and a cache miss? 5) Why does a cache bring in a whole block rather than a single value? 6) Why can we not build the whole machine from register-speed memory? Answers: 1) registers, cache, RAM, disk storage. 2) a recently used value is likely to be used again soon. 3) data near a recently used address is likely to be used soon. 4) on a hit the value is already in the cache and returns quickly; on a miss it must be fetched from a slower level. 5) to exploit spatial locality - neighboring data will probably be needed shortly, so fetching the block saves future misses. 6) it is too expensive and must be small and close to the processor, so large amounts of it are impractical.

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: assuming more memory always means a faster computer - speed depends far more on whether the data you need is near the processor than on the sheer size of memory. Mistake: confusing cache with storage; cache is small, fast, and temporary, while storage is large, slow, and persistent. Mistake: believing a cache miss fetches only the requested value, when it actually pulls in a surrounding block to serve expected nearby accesses. Mistake: thinking locality is a guarantee rather than a tendency; random access patterns can defeat it and leave programs stalling on memory. Exit ticket: (a) List the four main levels of the hierarchy from fastest to slowest. (b) Name and briefly define the two kinds of locality. Answers: registers, cache, main memory, and storage; temporal locality, where a recently used value is reused soon, and spatial locality, where nearby data is used soon after.

lessons.title: Pipelining, performance, input/output, and buses
lessons.grammar_note: Measure a processor by throughput and real work done, not by clock rate alone.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Explain how pipelining raises throughput, interpret basic performance measures like clock rate, and describe how the processor talks to the outside world over buses. Warm-up: if one instruction takes several steps, could the processor start the next instruction before the first one fully finishes? By the end you will be able to describe pipelining as an assembly line for instructions, distinguish latency from throughput, read what a clock rate does and does not tell you, name the common hazards that complicate pipelines, and explain the roles of the address, data, and control buses along with the idea of an input and output device. These ideas tie the processor and memory lessons together with the practical question of how fast real work actually gets done and how data physically moves between parts. Keep the fetch-decode-execute cycle in mind, since pipelining is simply overlapping copies of that cycle.

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: A clock is a steady pulse; its rate, measured in cycles per second, sets the pace of the processor. But clock rate alone does not decide speed, because instructions differ in how many cycles they need and in how well they overlap. Pipelining overlaps them like an assembly line: while one instruction is being executed, the next is being decoded and a third is being fetched, so a new instruction can finish almost every cycle even though each still takes several cycles end to end. Here latency is the time for one instruction to pass all the way through, while throughput is how many finish per unit time; pipelining improves throughput without shortening any single instruction's latency. Pipelines hit hazards - situations that stall the line, such as one instruction needing a result the previous one has not produced yet, or a branch whose direction is not yet known. Meanwhile the processor connects to memory and devices over buses: shared sets of wires that carry addresses, data, and control signals.

sections.heading: Key concepts & examples
sections.text: Imagine each instruction needs five steps and each step takes one cycle. Without pipelining, ten instructions take about 50 cycles. With a five-stage pipeline running smoothly, the first instruction finishes after 5 cycles and then one more finishes every cycle, so ten instructions take roughly 14 cycles - a large gain in throughput even though each instruction still has a 5-cycle latency. Hazards interrupt this ideal. If instruction B needs a value that instruction A is still computing, the pipeline may insert a brief stall. If a branch is taken, instructions already fetched after it may have to be discarded. Buses carry the traffic: the address bus names which location the processor wants, the data bus carries the value to or from it, and the control bus signals whether it is a read or a write. Input and output devices - a keyboard, a disk, a network card - attach through controllers on these buses, so reading a key and reading a memory cell look broadly similar to the processor.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: 1) What is the difference between latency and throughput? 2) In one phrase, what does pipelining do? 3) Give one example of a pipeline hazard. 4) What does the address bus carry, and what does the data bus carry? 5) Does a higher clock rate always mean a faster computer? 6) What does the control bus signal? Answers: 1) latency is the time for one instruction to complete; throughput is how many complete per unit time. 2) it overlaps the stages of consecutive instructions so one finishes almost every cycle. 3) an instruction needing a result not yet produced, or a branch whose outcome is not yet known. 4) the address bus carries which location is wanted; the data bus carries the actual value to or from it. 5) no - it helps, but real speed also depends on how many cycles instructions take, how well they pipeline, and how often the processor waits on memory. 6) whether the operation is a read or a write, among other control information.

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: judging a processor by clock rate alone - two chips at the same rate can differ widely because of pipelining, cache behavior, and how many cycles their instructions take. Mistake: thinking pipelining makes a single instruction finish faster; it raises throughput, not the latency of any one instruction. Mistake: assuming pipelines always run at full speed, when hazards force occasional stalls or discarded work. Mistake: confusing the three buses; the address bus names the location, the data bus moves the value, and the control bus says what kind of operation it is. Exit ticket: (a) Define latency and throughput and say which one pipelining improves. (b) Name the three buses and what each carries. Answers: latency is the time for one instruction to finish and throughput is the number finishing per unit time, and pipelining improves throughput; the address bus carries the target location, the data bus carries the value, and the control bus carries signals such as read or write.

items.translation: a tiny, very fast storage slot inside the processor, holding a value in use right now
items.example: The add instruction placed its result into register R1.

items.translation: small fast memory near the processor that keeps recently used data to avoid slow trips to RAM
items.example: The second pass over the array was fast because the data was already in the cache.

items.translation: the contract listing the instructions a processor supports and how each is encoded as a number
items.example: Two different chips can run the same program when they share an instruction set architecture.

items.translation: overlapping the stages of consecutive instructions, like an assembly line, to raise throughput
items.example: With pipelining a new instruction finishes almost every cycle, though each still takes several cycles.

lessons.title: Parallelism and how high-level code becomes something the hardware runs
lessons.grammar_note: A 'core' is hardware and a 'thread' is a stream of execution; keep the two words distinct.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Describe how multicore processors and threads let a computer do several things at once, and trace the path from high-level source code down to the instructions the hardware runs. Warm-up: if one processor core runs one stream of instructions at a time, how could a computer play music while you type? By the end you will be able to explain what a core and a thread are, describe the difference between doing tasks truly at the same time and merely switching between them quickly, and lay out the stages - compiling or interpreting, assembling, and loading - that turn a line of a high-level language into machine code in memory. This final lesson ties the whole course together, connecting the human-friendly programs you write to the fetch-decode-execute loop you now understand. It also sets up why writing parallel programs is harder than writing sequential ones.

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: A core is a complete processor capable of running its own stream of instructions. A multicore chip packs several cores together, so a computer can genuinely run multiple instruction streams at the same instant - true parallelism. A thread is a single such stream of execution within a program; a program may have several threads. Even a single core can appear to run many threads at once by switching between them rapidly, a trick called concurrency that is not the same as true parallelism. Running work in parallel can finish it sooner, but it introduces hard problems: threads that share data can interfere with one another, and coordinating them correctly takes care. Separately, the code you write in a high-level language is not what the hardware runs. A compiler translates that source into machine code ahead of time, or an interpreter reads and carries it out line by line as the program runs. Either way, the result is ultimately the numeric instructions the fetch-decode-execute loop consumes.

sections.heading: Key concepts & examples
sections.text: Trace a single line such as 'total = a + b' in a high-level language. A compiler first checks the line and translates it into assembly roughly like LOAD R1, a; LOAD R2, b; ADD R1, R2; STORE R1, total. An assembler then turns that assembly into machine code - the actual numbers. A loader places those numbers into memory, sets the program counter to the start, and the processor's fetch-decode-execute loop runs them, exactly as in the earlier lessons. An interpreted language skips the ahead-of-time step and instead has a running program read each statement and perform it immediately, though underneath it still drives the same hardware loop. For parallelism, imagine summing a huge array on a four-core chip: split the array into four parts, give each core one part to total, then add the four partial totals. Done carefully this is nearly four times faster; done carelessly, if two cores update one shared total at once, they can corrupt it - the classic hazard of shared data.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: 1) What is a processor core? 2) What is a thread? 3) What is the difference between true parallelism and concurrency on a single core? 4) What does a compiler do, and how does an interpreter differ? 5) In order, what stages turn a high-level line into running machine code in the compiled case? 6) Name one danger of parallel threads sharing data. Answers: 1) a complete processor that runs its own stream of instructions. 2) a single stream of execution within a program. 3) true parallelism runs multiple streams at the very same instant on separate cores, while concurrency on one core rapidly switches between streams to give the appearance of simultaneity. 4) a compiler translates source into machine code ahead of time, while an interpreter reads and carries out each statement as the program runs. 5) compile the source to assembly, assemble it into machine code, load it into memory, then the fetch-decode-execute loop runs it. 6) two threads updating the same value at once can corrupt it.

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: using 'core' and 'thread' as synonyms - a core is physical hardware that executes a stream, while a thread is a logical stream of execution that the hardware runs. Mistake: assuming concurrency means true parallelism; a single core can interleave many threads without ever running two at the same instant. Mistake: believing more cores always make a program proportionally faster, when shared-data coordination and parts that cannot be split limit the gain. Mistake: thinking high-level code runs directly on the hardware, when it must first be compiled or interpreted down to machine code. Exit ticket: (a) What is the difference between a core and a thread? (b) List, in order, the stages that take compiled high-level code to running machine code. Answers: a core is a complete processor that executes an instruction stream, while a thread is a single logical stream of execution; the stages are compile the source to assembly, assemble it into machine code, load it into memory, and run it through the fetch-decode-execute loop.
